Selling on Amazon without a support call

A Shopify-to-Amazon integration app's onboarding, redesigned so that merchants can succeed in listing products on Amazon independently

Company

CedCommerce

Role

Product Designer

Year

2023

Platform

Web · B2B

As with the original published case study, the flows and screens referenced here are conceptual reconstructions. The specific designs shipped for CedCommerce remain covered by an NDA and aren't reproduced.

On this page
Overview The problem Design process SolutionsImpact Learnings
Problem

Listing products was a daily struggle for merchants leading to 150–180 support calls per month (high operation cost beared for training implementation members) and high churn rate.

Solution

Personalised post onboarding step-by-step guidance on product listing based on seller type to make listing faster and easier for merchants and implementation members

Impact (projected)

20–30% reduction in monthly support calls and 50–60% increased usability of the app by merchants

01 · The problem

Support costs and churn, both traced to navigation.

CedCommerce's Amazon application runs as a plugin inside the Shopify application, letting Shopify sellers list their products on Amazon without leaving their existing storefront. It automates pushing Shopify listings to Amazon and syncs sales back — giving merchants a single place to manage both channels.

Syncing products led to many errors (Amazon product listing requirements), and fixing them was complicated, which frustrated merchants. Another significant issue identified after user research was that merchants were unsure how to navigate the application after onboarding, which often led them to call the customer support team and rely on them to fix errors and upload products on Amazon.

02 · Design process

How we reduced sellers' confusion.

Finding the root cause of the problem: To understand user issues, the following approaches were used:

  • Surveying CedCommerce's customer support team, comprising 55 members
  • Heuristic evaluation of the existing application's design
  • Competitor analysis to review offerings and app experience
  • Analyzing 10–15 client interaction videos provided by the support team, to understand the problem firsthand

Journey mapping: Mapping the merchant's path post-onboarding surfaced the same friction point across most conversations with support. Confusion set in immediately after signup, before a single product was live. That's what the two seller stories (see Solutions) were built from.

Consolidating insights into goals: The journey findings converged into two seller stories, each reframed as a design question to work from:

First-time seller

How might we guide first-time sellers step-by-step, so they can list products accurately and start selling with confidence?

Existing seller

How might we give existing sellers intuitive, in-app guidance to manage inventory, orders, and sales across Shopify and Amazon, seamlessly?

How did the current system look, post merchant onboarding: A heatmap review of the live Overview screen surfaced exactly where the friction was coming from:

  • Linear information flow: forced a lot of scrolling to get through the page
  • Text-heavy: dense copy where a glance should have sufficed
  • Unused space on the left: a large area doing nothing
  • No actionable urgency above the fold: nothing prompted merchants to act right away

Prioritization: Research turned up more possible fixes than a live product could absorb at once. A prioritization matrix sorted them by impact vs. effort, to decide what actually needed rebuilding first.

First direction — sync on onboarding Make the app work for the merchant immediately: on onboarding, existing sellers would have their products start syncing right away, and new sellers would be dropped into a step-by-step upload flow — delivering value from the very first screen.
The risk Longer onboarding times, API failures that could break uploads or syncing, and sync jobs that could run 30 minutes to an hour for larger catalogs — the same risks that were driving the support calls and churn this redesign was meant to fix.

The pivot: Pivoted to onboard sellers quickly and give merchants more control, through a step-by-step Listing Centre and Selling Guide process tailored to seller type. System-backed processes like product syncing also moved to the backend, running automatically rather than manually — so existing sellers could see value as soon as they onboarded.

03 · Solutions

Two sellers, two different needs.

User stories split the merchant base into two groups with different blockers:

First-time seller

Needs a guided, step-by-step path accurate enough to get first listings live without hand-holding from support.

Existing seller

Already has active listings; needs clearer in-app guidance to manage inventory, orders, and sales across Shopify and Amazon.

A

Selling Guide

Solves → first-time seller's guidance gap
  • Step-by-step guidance, tailored to first-time sellers: breaking the process into small steps with video tutorials. Progress indication to highlight and prompt completion.
  • Grid layout: Two column card layout, keeping the important actions surfaced above the fold
  • Visual cues over copy: Progress indication; short videos in place of dense text, highlight current step with color and primary call to action button.
B

Listing Centre & Action Center

Solves → existing seller's fragmented management
  • Listing Centre: templates, product details, and help docs consolidated into one place
  • Action Center: errors, alerts, and announcements split by priority, not by whatever surfaced first
  • Step-by-step template creation: faster attribute entry, fewer mistakes
04 · Impact

Reduced support calls and increased usability.

No measured post-launch data is available for this NDA-covered engagement — so this is stated as the redesign's goal, not a confirmed result.

↓ 150–180 / mo
Reduce the monthly support calls tied to app confusion, by removing the navigation friction driving them
05 · Learnings

What this project reinforced.

  • Cross-functional collaborationGetting to real root causes, and to solutions that fit the existing framework, required constant back-and-forth with support, product, and engineering — not just research handed off once.
  • Working in agile incrementsBreaking a large redesign into smaller, testable pieces — sequencing critical changes ahead of nice-to-haves — kept a live-product rework manageable.
  • Depth in PolarisWorking inside Shopify's design system built a much closer working knowledge of e-commerce conventions — modularity, accessibility, and responsive patterns included.
The takeaway

A redesign grounded in real support and usage data, built to let merchants succeed independently. The reduction in support calls is the goal this redesign was built to achieve.
